items.title: Explaining the Details Enhances Human Perceptions of the Persuasiveness of GAI Misinformation Corrections
items.abstract: Public apprehension regarding AI hallucination creates a substantial epistemic barrier, significantly undermining users’ perceived persuasiveness of GAI-based health corrections despite their technical accuracy. To navigate this challenge, this study integrates Fuzzy-Trace Theory and the Persuasion Knowledge Model to explore how the presentation of precise numbers alleviates skepticism to enhance the persuasiveness of GAI health misinformation corrections. Across three experiments (N = 588), we tested the proposed model. Presenting specific numbers along with the gist significantly enhances persuasiveness, while gist without numbers is comparatively less persuasive for an AI advisor. Perceived AI hallucination and cognitive fluency serially mediate the relationship between the presentation of numbers and the persuasiveness of GAI-generated health misinformation correction. Users’ thinking style (Analytic vs. Intuitive) moderates the relationship between perceived hallucination and cognitive fluency. These results provide guidance for designing GAI platforms that build trust by prioritizing transparent, data-rich explanations alongside clear communication of the gist of corrective information.

items.title: Exploring pre-service teachers’ conflict resolution strategies and decision-making patterns in AI-based multi-agent environments
items.abstract: Conflict resolution is essential for teachers. Pre-service teachers (PSTs) often struggle to connect coursework with classroom practice, especially in multi-role conflicts. Artificial intelligence (AI) simulations may offer a low-risk environment. This study examined PSTs’ conflict-resolution practices in an AI-based multi-agent setting where virtual participants were available within the same conflict scenario. We developed a chatbot through which 20 PSTs interacted with an aggressor, an accomplice, a victim, parents, and a tutor in a peer-conflict scenario. Using dialogue logs, we applied inductive qualitative content analysis and lag sequential analysis to examine behavioural transitions. The analysis identified two complementary findings. First, PSTs’ strategies varied by student-agent role. When addressing aggressors, they tended to use guiding reflection, emotional support, surface threat, and role endowment; when addressing accomplices, they more often used positive encouragement, guiding reflection, home-school collaboration, and emotional support; and when addressing victims, they relied on home-school collaboration, positive relationship guidance, and emotional support. Second, PSTs’ engagement with AI guidance followed four pathways: relying on AI-generated suggestions, iterative inquiry with AI, doubting AI-generated suggestions, and bypassing AI-generated suggestions. These findings suggest that PSTs selectively negotiated role-specific cues and AI guidance, making visible situated professional judgement in AI-supported conflict-resolution practice.

items.title: Fact construction as a missing layer in legal AI: a practice-grounded framework for evaluating multi-agent legal consultation
items.abstract: Legal AI research often evaluates large language models (LLMs) on legal reasoning tasks under the assumption that relevant facts are already structured and available. This assumption overlooks a prior and practically consequential stage of legal work: fact construction, namely the transformation of incomplete, fragmented, and interactionally disclosed information into coherent factual narratives. This study conceptualizes fact construction as a distinct evaluation layer in legal AI and introduces a practice-grounded framework for assessing it in AI-assisted legal consultation. Rather than proposing a legal advice system or doctrinal rule-matching architecture, we use a role-separated multi-agent workflow consisting of a fact-constrained Litigant Twin, a structured-questioning LegalAider, a NarrativeAgent for factual synthesis, and an Evaluator for factual-alignment assessment. Using 100 de-identified legal clinic consultation records, we evaluate multiple LLMs under rubric-based assessment, comparing generated factual narratives against original human-authored consultation records in terms of factual accuracy, completeness, and consistency. The results show that LLM-based agents can generate usable factual narratives under constrained conditions, particularly when cases are internally consistent, limited to a single dispute, and supported by clear actor-role relationships. However, cross-model evaluator agreement remains moderate, and outlier analysis reveals recurring structural sources of failure, including anonymization-induced referential ambiguity, third-party reporting, multi-episode case complexity, and numerically dense facts. These findings suggest that reliability in AI-assisted legal consultation depends not only on model capability, but also on interaction design, data representation, institutional record-keeping, and human oversight. By treating fact construction as a distinct analytical layer, this article contributes a practice-grounded framework for evaluating responsible LLM integration in legal settings and highlights the need for factual grounding, contestability, and human-supervised review before downstream legal analysis begins.

items.title: FALCA: Falsification-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Hierarchical Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Deep Search Agents
items.abstract: Long-horizon deep search requires LLM agents to iteratively decompose complex information needs, gather evidence from external sources, and maintain a reliable research state under multiple constraints. A central challenge is that early mistakes can be amplified over the search trajectory: agents may anchor on an incorrect candidate, collect partially supporting evidence, overlook contradictions, and accumulate errors that misguide subsequent reasoning. We propose FALCA, a falsification-aware framework that formulates deep search as a propose-falsify process. FALCA adopts a collaborative Searcher-Falsifier architecture, where the Searcher proposes candidate answers or sub-answers, while independent Falsifiers actively seek counterevidence, check unmet constraints, identify conflicts, and produce concise falsification reports for research-state revision. To strengthen this loop, we introduce falsification-aware training, combining SFT warmup on falsification trajectories with agentic RL based on parallel rollouts and hierarchical credit assignment over research stages, state transitions, and actions. Experiments on five search benchmarks show that FALCA improves long-horizon deep search performance over backbone and harness ablations, while reducing confirmation bias and error accumulation through more effective falsification and research-state revision.

items.title: Financial self efficacy as a mediator of artificial intelligence use in detecting money laundering and financial fraud in Jordanian Islamic banks
items.abstract: This study examines the mediating role of financial self-efficacy in the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and the perceived effectiveness of detecting money laundering and financial fraud in Jordanian Islamic banks. The study addresses a behavioral and institutional gap in the literature by explaining how AI-supported monitoring capabilities may be translated into effective regulatory action through employees’ confidence in interpreting and using AI-generated outputs. A quantitative cross-sectional survey design was adopted. Data were collected from 115 employees working in compliance, Shariah compliance, Shariah supervision, internal audit, auditing, and risk management functions in Jordanian Islamic banks. The questionnaire consisted of 35 items measuring AI adoption, financial self-efficacy, perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness, and demographic characteristics. The data were analyzed using reliability and validity tests, correlation analysis, standardized multiple regression, and regression-based mediation analysis. The results indicate that AI adoption has a statistically significant positive direct effect on perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness after accounting for financial self-efficacy (β = 0.296, p = 0.001). AI adoption also has a significant positive effect on financial self-efficacy ( β = 0.640, p < 0.001), while financial self-efficacy has a significant positive effect on perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness ( β = 0.491, p < 0.001). The mediation analysis shows a significant indirect effect of AI adoption on perceived detection effectiveness through financial self-efficacy (indirect effect = 0.314, Sobel z = 4.806, p < 0.001). The VAF value of 51.46% indicates complementary partial mediation. The findings suggest that AI adoption contributes to perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness not only through technological capabilities but also through employees’ financial self-efficacy. The study recommends integrating AI-supported monitoring systems with structured training, human-in-the-loop governance, and Shariah-sensitive regulatory procedures in Islamic banks.

items.title: Firms, competition, and market structure
items.abstract: This chapter examines artificial intelligence (AI) as a force that reorganizes firms, platforms, and market structure. AI affects competition not only by lowering costs, but also by changing the industrial assets that matter: proprietary data, compute infrastructure, model capability, specialized talent, distribution channels, and the ability to run continuous experiments. The chapter explains why AI can reinforce superstar firm dynamics, how data can generate increasing returns without being a simple monopoly input, and why platform markets require a two-sided rather than purely product market view. It also studies algorithmic pricing and the possibility that learning systems may facilitate collusive outcomes even without explicit human agreement. The central message is deliberately balanced: AI may intensify concentration when feedback loops between users, data, models, and capital are strong, but it can also lower entry barriers when general-purpose models, cloud infrastructure, and open-source tools become broadly accessible. The policy problem is therefore not to punish scale as such, but to distinguish productive scale from exclusionary control over the bottlenecks of the AI economy.

items.title: From “how” to learn to “what” to learn in multiagent systems and robotics
items.abstract: Abstract There remains much more to Artificial Intelligence than understanding how to learn with neural networks. Inspired in part by how babies, and humans in general, tend to choose for themselves what (and when ) to learn in addition to how to learn, this article discusses similar opportunities, in the areas of multiagent systems and robotics. Grounded in past research on the topic, it categorizes opportunities for choosing what to learn as coming from task decomposition or simplification for difficult problems and/or large environments; unsupervised pre‐training of representations and priors; multiagent learning; and learning from human interaction. The article is based closely on a keynote talk with the same title, delivered at the AAAI‐2026 conference in Singapore on January 22nd, 2026.

items.title: From AI labels to trust: cognitive pathways linking authenticity judgments, risk perception, and trust in AI-generated videos
items.abstract: Background The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) has raised concerns regarding the authenticity and trustworthiness of synthetic media. Although AI disclosure labels are increasingly used as transparency mechanisms, the cognitive processes through which these cues influence trust formation remain unclear. Objective This study aimed to develop and test a cognitive pathway model explaining how AI disclosure labels, authenticity judgments, perceived risk, cognitive processing styles, and literacy factors shape trust toward AI-generated videos. Methods A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted with 617 participants randomly assigned to four conditions involving AI-generated instructional videos with different AI label and video quality combinations. Participants evaluated authenticity, systematic and heuristic processing, trust, perceived risk, adoption intention, sharing intention, AI literacy, and media literacy. Regression, bootstrapped mediation, and moderation analyses were performed. Results AI disclosure labels significantly reduced perceived authenticity but did not directly affect trust, adoption, sharing intention, or perceived risk. Trust formation occurred through cognitive pathways: systematic processing increased trust, whereas heuristic processing reduced trust. Authenticity enhanced trust and lowered perceived risk, with perceived risk mediating the authenticity–trust relationship. Trust positively predicted adoption and sharing intentions, while AI and media literacy moderated selected relationships. Conclusion Trust in AI-generated videos was not directly determined by transparency labels alone. Instead, the observed associations among authenticity judgments, perceived risk, information processing, and trust were consistent with a multi-stage cognitive interpretation, although the cross-sectional post-exposure measurement of these constructs does not establish their temporal or causal sequence.

items.title: From AI models to AI agents: governance through recursive oversight and revocable access
items.abstract: Recent developments in AI are shifting the main source of risk from the flawed outputs of individual models to the unintended effects of agentic AI systems. Limited but growing evidence of misaligned behavior in swarms of AI agents suggests that such systems can pursue unassigned tasks and act beyond the reach of traditional corporate governance tools, which presuppose agents with interests, fiduciary duties and legal personality. This paper argues that the object of governance should be expanded from the model in isolation to the agentic AI system as a whole, and that oversight should be calibrated to the combined level of capability, autonomy, external access, permissions and scale. It proposes a framework of recursive governance, in which monitoring, evaluation, intervention and authorization form a continuous feedback loop rather than a fixed checklist. Four propositions follow: (P1) governance must become more stringent as capability and operational autonomy combine with external access and scale; (P2) autonomous deployment at a given capability level should not occur unless predefined criteria for evaluation, monitoring, containment and independent verification are met; (P3) some governance functions should be embedded in the technical architecture rather than being left solely to ex post human intervention; (P4) enforcement should rest on conditional and revocable access to the infrastructure that autonomous operation requires, with the kill switch as the last resort of a broader regime, and should be anchored as far as possible to institutions, rules and forms of self-regulation that already exist. To this end, the paper proposes a three-stage enforcement architecture: (i) a lean, independent multilateral agency, composed mainly of experts in advanced AI, certifies that the governance process for AI agents is actually followed; (ii) the certificate is fully incorporated into the ESG framework already operating in the European Union and linked to existing EU legislation on sustainability reporting, sustainable finance and ESG ratings; (iii) the IMF includes AI governance compliance in its periodic surveillance of member countries through the Financial Sector Assessment Program (FSAP). Apart from the new agency, which to our knowledge does not yet exist, enforcement would thus rely on institutions that are already in place. The proposed policies are framed as responses to three market failures: information asymmetry, negative externalities and a collective action problem among competing developers (a safety race to the bottom). The last of these is to be addressed through common safety standards, not through any relaxation of antitrust rules.

items.title: From AI-Assisted Performance to Independent Thinking: A Framework for Developing Higher-Order Thinking with Generative AI in Higher Education
items.abstract: In an AI-supported task, a student may explain a weak comparison once it has been identified, yet fail to notice a similar problem without a reminder. A decision about further help therefore needs evidence about what the student did without being prompted. We examine such decisions in English-medium university argumentation and evidence evaluation. The framework brings together English-language work on scaffolding, learner-generated reasoning, metacognitive calibration, and cognitive offloading. We distinguish help that supplies a reason from help that initiates a check. Readiness to work without the first does not establish readiness to work without the second. Coding examples and boundary cases make evidence about these functions interpretable, while six conditional propositions connect reconstruction and regulation to adaptation and transfer. A proposed experiment gives every group comparable diagnostic practice but varies whether teachers use its results to adjust assistance. This comparison isolates the value of using the evidence from learning through the diagnostic task itself. We relate the account to four GenAI approaches and illustrate it with a hypothetical sociology lesson. Help may be retained or restored when a new task requires it. The framework and coding rules need validation, particularly beyond the language and disciplinary settings considered here.

items.title: From disrupted routines to sustainable practice: integrating management sciences to navigate the innovation journey of precision imaging
items.abstract: Precision medicine is reshaping medical imaging through artificial intelligence, quantitative biomarkers or hybrid modalities such as PET-CT. Yet these tools reach patients unevenly, and that unevenness is usually blamed on technical problems: interoperability, validation, trust. Drawing on management science and the sociology of professions, we propose a different explanation. What decides whether an innovation reaches patients equitably is not the technology, but the way it travels. We distinguish three ways of travelling. Diffusion is spontaneous spread through professional networks (letting it happen). Dissemination is spread deliberately directed towards a defined population (helping it happen). Implementation is the work of turning an adopted innovation into everyday routine (making it happen). Imaging innovations have travelled mainly by diffusion, which follows existing specialist density, funding rules and like-with-like professional networks; diffusion therefore reproduces the inequalities of access it inherits instead of correcting them. Three consequences follow. First, adoption hides three separate decisions taken by different people: acquiring the equipment, deciding what the examination actually contains, and deciding whether it is requested at all. Routine statistics count the first and the third; the second is never measured. Second, professional boundaries are held in place at once by regulation, by specialty jurisdiction and by everyday working relationships, so reforms acting on only one of them fail. Third, the medical report is where those boundaries meet: when it does not carry an integrated answer, the innovation stalls. A fourth point runs through all three: an innovation's value is not fixed before it travels; its construction is predicated on the expectations that precede it, and the practices through which it is utilised. Using a three-study programme on PET-CT in France as illustration, we argue that equitable and sustainable precision imaging is achieved not by buying equipment but by governing how innovations spread—including by actively retiring the low-value practices they were meant to replace, what management science calls exnovation.

items.title: From Encoding to Generation: Towards Empathetic Large Language Models
items.abstract: Empathetic interaction involves two distinguishable capacities: representing another person's emotional state (cognitive empathy) and generating an appropriate response to that state (affective empathy). We apply this distinction to examine how emotion-related information is internally organized, selectively attended to, and carried through response generation in Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct across 10 emotion categories from the EmpatheticDialogues dataset. Layer-wise linear probing revealed a broad middle-layer region of peak emotion-category decodability, with the layer-11 L2 probe achieving 63.6% held-out accuracy against a 10% chance level and a 54.6% TF-IDF lexical baseline. During response generation, emotion-related user tokens received 1.89 times as much attention per token as other utterance tokens, concentrated across layers 10-15. Target-emotion alignment then decreased from a mean cosine similarity of 0.239 for input representations to 0.125 for generated responses, with positive drift in 77% of examples and the largest shifts for angry and furious. Emotion-category representation, attention allocation, and response-level alignment therefore emerge as distinguishable components of model processing that can be analyzed through a functional cognitive-affective empathy framework. These findings provide a foundation for monitoring emotion representations during generation and leveraging models' existing affective structure to support more naturally empathetic responses without relying on external prompting or explicit emotion conditioning.

items.title: From joy to resistance: consumer reactions to disclosure of AI-created advertisements
items.abstract: Conventional wisdom suggests that viewers tend to evaluate AI-generated advertisements negatively. We argue that viewers can nevertheless enjoy creative advertisements produced by AI. However, the belief that creativity is an exclusively human attribute may prompt cognitive regulation when AI involvement is disclosed. Using a consumer neuroscience approach, we conducted a one-factor, three-level between-subjects experiment in which participants viewed advertisements with no disclosure, disclosure of human–AI collaboration, or disclosure of full AI creation. Creative advertisements elicited joy, captured by facial expression analysis, regardless of whether they were created by humans or AI. Greater joy was associated with less message counterarguing and more favourable advertisement attitudes, but only in the absence of AI disclosure. These findings suggest that AI disclosure does not diminish initial enjoyment. Instead, it may act as a persuasion knowledge cue that activates cognitive regulation, leading viewers to override their positive affective responses when subsequently evaluating the advertisement.

items.title: From Predictive Geometry to Action: Learning Complementary Predictive Representations for Embodied Manipulation
items.abstract: Effective manipulation requires a policy to capture not only about the current scene geometry, but also about how that geometry will evolve under interaction. Existing approaches either augment policies with geometric information from current observations or introduce future prediction as auxiliary supervision, leaving open how predictive geometry should be represented for action generation. Therefore, we propose a two-stage framework, which learns complementary predictive representations from multi-view video clips. During pretraining, a frozen 3D foundation model provides dense geometric features that are compressed into predictive geometric representations and optimized to preserve scene structure and its temporal evolution. Action supervision is then applied to geometric transitions to extract a complementary motor representation that emphasizes action-relevant transitions. During downstream post-training, predictive geometry is transferred through geometry queries, while the motor representation guides intermediate features along the action-generation pathway. Future observations are used only as privileged supervision during training and are not required at inference time. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv, and real-world bimanual and single-arm tasks, our approach consistently improves downstream policies, including an absolute gain of 10.4 percentage points on the WidowX evaluation. We further demonstrate transfer across multiple VLA architectures and WAMs, with improvements in both future-world and action prediction. The code will be available at https://github.com/xuxiaoxxxx/CPR.

items.title: From Prompting to Direct Manipulation: Interaction Patterns and Designer Experience in Generative AI-Supported Visual Workflows
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now employed in many visual design programs to create images rapidly, but these images may not meet the designer's expectations at first glance. This paper studies mismatch via text prompting, parameters and presets, reference-based input, and in-canvas manipulation. The fourteen academic sources in the review include thirteen peer-reviewed publications from 2024-2026 and Shneiderman's original work on direct manipulation. The workflow stage, participant group, interaction pattern, and the five dimensions of efficiency, perceived control, cognitive load, creative agency, and output predictability were used for evidence coding. Based on this evidence, the demand for refinement reduces the apparent advantage of rapid exploration. Effort saved in generation may be recovered by reducing prompt modifications, filtering output, or re-retrieving a suitable image. More local interactions help express and observe the decisions, but they do not eliminate the uncertainty in the generated results. Evidence for the parameters and presets is relatively scarce, so all four patterns cannot be evaluated equally. This framing clarifies how interface design, rather than model capability alone, affects professional agency and supports more informed tool selection in creative practice.

items.title: From Repositories to Ecosystems: The Strategic Evolution, Institutional Practices, and Policy Frameworks of Open Educational Resource Initiatives in Higher Education
items.abstract: Open Educational Resources (OER) in higher education are shifting from models centred on the creation and storage of learning materials towards structures characterised by greater connectivity and institutionalisation. This study analyses this development across four dimensions: the emergence of repositories; infrastructure connectivity and interoperability; the institutionalisation of OER in association with Open Educational Practices (OEP); and the formation of adaptive OER ecosystems. Drawing on a review and mapping of the literature, policy analysis, and a comparison of selected prominent OER initiatives, the study conceptualises the development of OER as a five-level progression: repository, organised production, institutionalisation, ecosystem, and adaptive/AI-enabled ecosystem. The findings indicate that repositories constitute a necessary infrastructural condition, but are insufficient in themselves to ensure the effective use, reuse, and sustainability of OER. Interoperability, stakeholder capacities, pedagogical practices, policies, and governance mechanisms become increasingly important as OER expands. Accordingly, the study argues that an OER ecosystem should be understood as a structure comprising interconnected components that can adapt to technological change, particularly the development of generative AI.

items.title: From Scorecards to Agents: A Survey of Anti-Fraud Models Across the Model-Risk Boundary, with a Focus on Evidence Traceability
items.abstract: The revised United States guidance on model risk management, issued in April 2026, applies its principles to traditional statistical and quantitative models and to non-generative, non-agentic AI models, and places generative and agentic AI explicitly outside its scope. This survey follows the models used against fraud and financial crime across that line, from rules, scorecards, and statistical tests, through non-generative machine learning, to generative models and language-model agents, across six fraud types. Unlike prior surveys, we place all three generations in one decision-theoretic frame: we restate in one notation known results on cost-optimal and capacity-constrained alerting, undersampling calibration, and the identifiability of recall from alert feedback, express each generation's model, explanation, and validation quantity in that frame, and add two stylized models, one showing why mean aggregation dilutes the neighborhood signal of camouflaged fraudsters and one showing how verifier independence bounds the residual errors in a generated narrative. We find that statistical models and non-generative machine learning have mature validation practice anchored in supervisory guidance, that generative AI now appears both as a tool of fraudsters and as a component of defenses, and that in hybrid pipelines the generative component can write what an analyst or examiner reads although no dedicated supervisory framework covers it. We therefore formalize the evidence-traceability controls that can supply this missing validation as a division of verification labor, between the drafting agent, a deterministic field check, an independent verifier and the human examiner, governed by three parameters an institution can estimate; we then compare the generations quantity by quantity and close with a research agenda.

items.title: From the Network Society to Synthetic Communication: A Comparative Media Ecology Analysis of the Communication Regimes of Generations Z, Alpha, and Beta
items.abstract: This study comparatively examines the communication environments and practices of Generations Z, Alpha, and Beta within the framework of media ecology. Generations are treated not as biological age cohorts but as experiential and epistemic regimes shaped by the dominant communication medium. The study is not an empirical field investigation but offers a conceptual and typological comparison. It draws on established empirical literature for Generation Z, platform and interface studies along with child and media research for Generation Alpha, and critical discourse analysis of technology vision texts and the sociotechnical imaginaries approach for Generation Beta. The comparison proceeds along five parameters namely dominant medium, mode of interaction, content production model, epistemic authority, and socio-communicative role. The findings suggest a gradual shift in communication from network-based human-to-human interaction toward human-artificial intelligence interaction and a relocation of epistemic authority from peer groups and algorithmic feeds to personalized artificial intelligence agents. The study argues that this shift necessitates reconsidering the sender-receiver model alongside actor-network theory and the human-machine communication literature.

items.title: From Tokens to Files: Multi-Granularity Detection and Localization of AI-Involved Code
items.abstract: The increasing use of large language models for code generation calls for methods that distinguish purely human-written code from AI-involved code: files in which any part, however small, was generated or substantially modified by a model. Beyond flagging such files, we aim to localize the lines or blocks attributable to AI. Existing approaches compress a file into a single score, from surface stylistic features or a global code representation, which averages away the evidence when only a few blocks are AI-involved. We propose a framework that models AI authorship at the token level and predicts at the line, block, and file levels. A frozen code language model is equipped with two low-rank adapters, trained separately on machine-written and human-written files; their per-token log-likelihood ratio provides local evidence of AI authorship. Lightweight heads aggregate this evidence within lines and blocks, using the surrounding code context, and their local predictions are aggregated into a file-level decision. We train on mixed-authorship files built from human originals and their AI-generated or AI-modified counterparts, including continuation and fill-in-the-middle scenarios. On an internal test set of 11,773 AI-involved files across six generation regimes against 2,541 human files, our method reaches 72.4 macro F1 at a 1% FPR operating point. With no adaptation, it reaches 62.5 line-level F1 on HybridCodeAuthorship, an external human-AI co-writing benchmark with no training split, above the 56 its own paper reports as the best line-level result. On 19,445 human-written files from repositories created before 2022, the false-positive rate stays between 0.55% and 0.81% under the transported 1% threshold, so the operating point holds on real human code.

items.title: Fundamentals of Natural Language Processing and Large Language Models
items.abstract: This chapter introduces the fundamental principles of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Large Language Models (LLMs) within the context of Sports Science and data-driven analytics. It demonstrates how unstructured textual and vocal data complement traditional numerical performance metrics by capturing contextual, psychological, and communicative aspects of sport environments. The chapter systematically presents core NLP techniques, including tokenization, lemmatization, sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, topic modeling, and word embeddings, and explains their role in transforming language-based data into structured representations for performance analysis and decision-making. Building on these foundations, the chapter examines key neural network architectures used in NLP, particularly recurrent neural networks, Long Short-Term Memory models, and Transformer-based systems. Special emphasis is placed on the attention mechanism and its role in enabling scalable and context-aware language modelling. The chapter further analyzes the capabilities and limitations of Large Language Models, including their generative potential, adaptability through fine-tuning and prompt-based interaction, and challenges such as hallucinations, bias, and interpretability. Through multimodal integration and applied case studies, the chapter highlights how NLP and LLMs contribute to sports analytics, athlete monitoring, talent identification, and real-time decision-making.

items.title: Future Machines on the Moon: Robotic Autonomy, Human Supervision and the Emerging Security Dimension of Lunar Operations
items.abstract: Lunar exploration has shifted from single flights to a planned buildup of permanent infrastructure. NASA flew four astronauts around the Moon on Artemis II in April 2026, and within eight weeks announced the first three robotic Moon Base missions along with close to a billion dollars in contracts for surface rovers, cargo landers and hopping drones. A parallel programme led by China and Russia, the International Lunar Research Station, is working towards a basic configuration by 2035 with a nuclear power unit delivered between 2033 and 2035. This paper examines the machines that will carry out most of the work in both programmes. It sets out the supervised autonomy model that governs how humans and robots divide decisions under communication delay, identifies the specific artificial intelligence techniques that lunar robots depend on, and proposes an interaction protocol for surface operations. The paper then turns to security. Nearly every capability needed for lunar construction, survey and resource extraction has an obvious military application, and the argument advanced here is that any confrontation on the Moon would be short, machine-led and fought over access to a small number of usable sites rather than over territory in the terrestrial sense. Gaps in the Outer Space Treaty and in the Artemis Accords are assessed against that prospect.

items.title: Gamificación y motivación estudiantil: desafíos y oportunidades
items.abstract: Introduction: Gamification incorporates game design elements into educational activities and offers opportunities to strengthen student participation. However, its effects depend on planning, curricular objectives and implementation conditions. The aim was to analyse its relationship with student motivation and identify opportunities and challenges relevant to Ecuadorian upper secondary education. Methodology: A narrative review of twenty publications on motivational foundations, gamification and learning was developed, incorporating international contributions and a review situated in Ecuador. The synthesis addressed four dimensions: foundations, motivation, pedagogical opportunities and implementation challenges. Published findings were distinguished from teaching guidance derived from their interpretation. Results: The reviewed meta-analyses report favourable, although variable, effects on cognitive, motivational and behavioural outcomes. Evidence specifically concerning intrinsic motivation indicates a small effect, alongside improvements in autonomy and relatedness and a smaller effect on perceived competence. Feedback, progressive challenges and collaboration offer pedagogical possibilities, whereas controlling rewards, exclusionary competition, access barriers and assessment restricted to points require attention. Conclusions: Gamification can enrich teaching when game elements are linked to verifiable learning and inclusive participation opportunities. Its application to Ecuadorian upper secondary education requires contextual adaptation and assessment of understanding and sustained motivation. The narrative approach and diversity of sources limit generalisation and do not permit attribution of effects to specific institutions or causal conclusions about the Ecuadorian school context.

items.title: GBClaw: An agentic AI framework for atomistic grain boundary research and mechanistic discovery
items.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems hold immense potential for automating complex workflows in materials discovery and design, but extending them to domain-intensive mechanistic investigations remains challenging. Here, we present GBClaw, an agentic AI framework for investigating the structure and deformation of general grain boundaries (GBs). Although general GBs constitute the vast majority of real-world interfaces in polycrystalline materials, they remain understudied because their structural complexity and interfacial mismatch complicate experimental and modeling research. GBClaw integrates large language models (LLMs) into a modular architecture comprising an orchestrator, specialized agents, domain-specific tools, simulation interfaces, and hierarchical memory. Through dynamic replanning and iterative workflow refinement, the framework effectively connects systematic simulations with targeted mechanistic analysis. Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt GBs in nickel, GBClaw characterized interfacial defect structures and identified diverse deformation modes across these incommensurate boundaries. Comparing boundary sliding with and without secondary GB misfit dislocations revealed substantial differences in shear strength, underscoring the critical role of defect hierarchies in sliding resistance. Furthermore, researcher-guided follow-up calculations traced an anomalously high shear resistance to metastable boundary structures. This work demonstrates that combining agentic AI with domain expertise bridges high-throughput computational screening with deep physical understanding of complex material interfaces.

items.title: Gender and Age Effects of Artificial Intelligence Narrator on Cultural Belonging and Comprehensibility in Heritage Museums
items.abstract: Heritage museums balance a dual mission: preserving culture and providing educational experiences. As institutions adopt AI-generated audio guides, narrator acoustic features—such as gender and age—significantly impact visitor experiences. This study examines how AI narrator gender and age influence Korean-English bilingual youths’ (ages 15–24) perceptions across two domains: the cultural function (belonging and empathy) and the educational function (comprehensibility and professionalism). Utilizing a between-subjects design, 71 participants were randomly assigned to one of four AI voice conditions (young/old, female/male) to evaluate audio guides for two heritage sites (Korea’s Geunjeongjeon and France’s Hall of Mirrors). A two-way ANOVA revealed older voices yielded significantly higher scores across both functions. For the educational function, male voices independently scored higher than females. For the cultural function, a significant interaction emerged, with older male voices scoring highest. These findings demonstrate that AI voices are not merely neutral information-delivery tools, but active social cues that shape cultural resonance and credibility. Older voices were associated with higher perceived educational and cultural function ratings, while older male voices received the highest cultural-function rating. Consequently, the study suggests that museums must move beyond default voice settings and strategically align AI personas with specific communicative goals.

items.title: Generative AI and Social Inequality in Education: A Human-Centered Social Science Review of Global and Indonesian Evidence
items.abstract: This review examined how generative artificial intelligence (AI) can widen educational opportunity while also reproducing social inequality. An integrative review synthesized 24 sources: 17 Indonesian publications (2022–2026), identified through national journal portals and Google Scholar, and seven international policy documents and scholarly works (2016–2023) selected as conceptual anchors. Thematic analysis produced four themes: unequal access, unequal digital and AI literacy, unequal capacity to benefit from AI-supported learning, and governance risks involving privacy, bias, academic integrity, and human agency. The reported benefits of generative AI, such as tutoring, writing support, and translation, appear to depend on connectivity, devices, language resources, teacher competence, and students' ability to evaluate machine output. The Indonesian evidence is mostly cross-sectional, self-reported, or based on small single-institution samples, with little evidence on learning outcomes. One national household analysis of school participation (not AI use) found no significant difference between 3T (disadvantaged, frontier, and outermost) and matched non-3T households, suggesting that regional labels may be an imperfect proxy for household conditions. The review proposes a cumulative model of AI inequality that extends van Dijk's sequence of digital inequality with a governance stage and a feedback loop. The model is a conceptual proposition, not a tested result, and recommendations are ordered by the strength of supporting evidence.

items.title: Generative AI as a team moderator in CSCL : Facilitating students' multidimensional engagement through adaptive scaffolding for socially shared regulation of learning
items.abstract: Abstract Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is essential for successful collaboration, yet effectively scaffolding it remains challenging because regulatory needs are dynamic and context‐dependent. While generative AI (GenAI) offers potential for adaptive support, current applications in collaborative learning largely position it as a content‐oriented tutor for knowledge explanation or idea generation, leaving its role as a process‐oriented team moderator for scaffolding SSRL processes underexplored. To address this gap, we conducted a 16‐week quasi‐experiment with 64 undergraduates in China, comparing adaptive SSRL scaffolding delivered by a GenAI agent in the adaptive‐SSRL condition with static scaffolding via structured digital worksheets in the static‐SSRL condition. Survey data and group discussion transcripts were analysed using statistical methods and epistemic network analysis. Results indicated several differences in students' multidimensional engagement between the two conditions: (1) Behaviourally, the adaptive‐SSRL group showed significantly higher participation equality, although participation intensity did not differ significantly between groups. (2) Cognitively, the adaptive‐SSRL group demonstrated deeper cognitive engagement, reflected in more advanced cognitive presence phases and more integrative, solution‐oriented discourse patterns. (3) Emotionally, the adaptive‐SSRL group reported significantly higher overall emotional engagement, particularly feeling more relaxed during collaboration and more connected with peers. These findings extend human–AI collaboration research by showing that GenAI can function as an SSRL‐informed team moderator rather than a content‐oriented tutor. They also offer design implications for GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding and human–AI role division in CSCL. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is critical for successful collaboration and is closely associated with the quality of student engagement. While static scaffolds (eg, worksheets) provide a basic regulatory structure, they fail to adapt to the dynamic and emergent needs of collaborating teams. Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used for personalised content support, yet its potential as a process‐oriented team moderator remains underexplored. What this paper adds This study introduced SSRLAgent, a GenAI agent grounded in SSRL theory and established principles of collective metacognitive support, to provide adaptive and interactive regulatory scaffolding. In a 16‐week quasi‐experiment, we compared GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding (SSRLAgent) with static scaffolding (structured digital worksheets) in CSCL. Adaptive‐SSRL scaffolding was associated with higher‐quality engagement: greater participation equality, deeper cognitive engagement and higher overall emotional engagement. Implications for practice and/or policy The study underscores the necessity of shifting SSRL scaffolding from static, ‘one‐size‐fits‐all’ support to adaptive GenAI interventions to improve collaborative engagement. The findings provide design guidance for developing SSRL agents that are embedded in the shared interaction space and responsive to groups' moment‐to‐moment regulatory needs. The study suggests a productive human–AI division of labour: GenAI agents can support process coordination and regulatory prompting, while teachers and peers remain essential for relationally complex forms of support that collaborative learning requires.

items.title: Generative AI Driven Cultural Content Production Mechanisms and Creative Labor Substitution Effects
items.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping content production in the cultural and creative industries by shifting cultural material organization, script writing, exhibition interpretation, and cultural tourism communication from linear manual workflows to human-AI collaborative workflows. Focusing on productivity improvement and the boundary of creative labor substitution, this research constructs a three-group comparison framework involving human-only creation, AI-assisted creation, and fully AI-generated creation. Based on public cultural heritage data, cultural policy texts, and cultural tourism communication samples from 2018 to 2024, LLMs, RAG, Sentence-BERT semantic retrieval, expert scoring, and mixed-effects ANOVA are combined to measure generation quality, policy suitability, and substitution intensity across different cultural tasks. The results show that the average completion time of the AI-assisted group decreases from 44.2 min to 25.7 min, while the overall quality score increases from 82.6 to 84.1, indicating that human-AI collaboration can improve production efficiency while maintaining content quality. Although the fully AI-generated group achieves the lowest time cost, its policy suitability and cultural accuracy decline noticeably. Task complexity further affects substitution intensity. Cultural tourism copy and short-video scripts are more substitutable, while exhibition interpretation and policy explanation still rely on human judgment. These findings provide quantitative evidence for AI adoption, creative labor restructuring, and cultural policy governance.

items.title: Generative AI in clinical practice: how should rheumatologists evaluate and monitor emerging tools?
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in rheumatology practice, to assist with tasks such as documentation, record summarization, and clinical decision support. Rheumatologists need a practical approach to determining what evidence and oversight each application requires. This narrative review proposes a framework based on two dimensions: contextual complexity and influence on patient care. Greater contextual complexity can make errors harder to detect, whereas greater influence on care increases the potential consequences of an undetected error. We examine evidence for workflow benefits and clinical effectiveness within this framework and consider safety, equity, privacy, governance, and implementation. Existing evidence on the benefits, accuracy and reliability of AI applications remains mixed. For example, studies of ambient AI scribes suggest reduced documentation burden, but evidence of improved patient outcomes from applications supporting clinical decisions is more limited. For applications with limited clinical influence, evaluation has initially focused on workflow, usability, and documentation quality. Tools that synthesize longitudinal information require additional assessment of completeness and source traceability. Those influencing diagnosis or treatment require prospective evaluation of clinical benefit and safety. Relevant vendor evidence should be assessed alongside proportionate local testing and ongoing monitoring. Safeguards should address risks such as hallucinations, automation bias, and propagating documentation errors, with attention to performance across patient groups. Changes in functionality or clinical use should prompt reassessment. The framework provides a structured basis for adoption decisions and identifies priorities for research on patient outcomes and feasible oversight in routine rheumatology care.

items.title: Generative AI Tools for Performance Assessment of University Students: Effects, Challenges, and Countermeasures
items.abstract: Against the backdrop of educational evaluation reform, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) has been increasingly applied to performance assessment, yet its actual effects and challenges remain underexplored. This study surveyed 50 undergraduate students to examine their perceptions of GAI-based performance assessment across five dimensions: evaluation efficiency and feedback timeliness, accuracy and fairness, appropriateness of scoring criteria and weight distribution, stability and trust, and deep learning and innovation. Results show that over 70% of respondents recognized GAI's advantages in scoring speed and feedback timeliness, and most regarded its scoring criteria as clear and consistent. However, nearly 75% believed GAI failed to identify innovative highlights, over 70% perceived a tendency to emphasize form over content, and 44% reported that such preferences constrained their creative expression. Respondents also raised concerns about incorrect information, technical instability, and the lack of emotional interaction compared with human evaluation. These findings suggest that GAI should act as an auxiliary tool rather than a full replacement for teacher evaluation. To address current limitations, it is necessary to improve GAI's deep evaluation and fact-checking capabilities, establish human-machine collaborative review mechanisms, and cultivate students' critical thinking. This study provides implications for integrating GAI into university performance assessment.

items.title: Generative AI-Based Virtual Hand Skin Tone and Nail Art Color Harmony: An Integrative Review Toward Personalized Nail Color Selection Guidelines
items.abstract: Nail art has evolved from a decorative beauty practice into a personalized cosmetic service that reflects individual image, style, and self-expression. Nevertheless, nail color selection remains largely dependent on personal preference, fashion trends, social-media images, and practitioner experience rather than standardized color-harmony criteria. This integrative review examines how objective skin color science, nail art design characteristics, personal color concepts, and generative artificial intelligence (AI) can be combined to establish a methodological basis for personalized nail color selection. The literature on human skin color measurement, CIELAB colorimetry, color-difference analysis, personal color and nail color matching, virtual beauty technologies, and skin-tone bias in AI-generated imagery was synthesized. The evidence supports representing hand skin color as a multidimensional profile based on L*, a*, b*, chroma, and hue angle rather than relying solely on warm/cool or seasonal categories. Nail art should likewise be described using colorimetric, optical, reflective, decorative, and compositional features. Generative AI offers a scalable means of creating standardized virtual hand–nail stimuli, but current evidence demonstrates substantial skin-tone imbalance and potential color inaccuracy in generated images. We therefore propose a six-stage framework: hand skin-color profiling, nail-art feature classification, generative AI-based virtual image generation, colorimetric accuracy and bias validation, skin–nail harmony modeling, and personalized guideline development. This framework should be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than as a validated recommendation system. External validation using objectively measured human hand skin color and perceptual evaluation is required before clinical, commercial, or professional implementation.

items.title: Generative AI-related employment threat, AI optimism, and employment anxiety among domestic and international students at a Chinese university
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the labor market, yet it remains unclear whether students’ appraisal of AI-driven employment threat translates into employment anxiety in similar ways across cultural groups. This study administered an online questionnaire to 1,595 domestic students (1,095) and international students (500) enrolled at Central South University. Perceived AI replacement threat, AI optimism, and employment anxiety were assessed with 13 five-point Likert items. Information channels, coping behaviors, desired institutional support, and perceived coping relief were assessed as supplementary measures. Confirmatory factor analyses supported an acceptable three-factor structure in both groups. The distinction between threat and anxiety remained qualified due to their substantial association. Metric invariance was established, and partial scalar invariance was obtained after the intercept of Q21 was freed. Perceived AI replacement threat and employment anxiety remained empirically distinguishable, although their latent correlation was stronger among international students than among domestic students. In the structural model, threat was strongly associated with anxiety ( β = 0.764) and weakly associated with optimism ( β = 0.133). After threat was included, optimism showed a small negative conditional association with anxiety ( β = −0.152). The indirect association through optimism was negative but limited in magnitude, and equivalent cross-sectional specifications fit the data equally well. This pattern is best interpreted as an exploratory statistical finding compatible with suppression, rather than confirmed evidence of a directional psychological mechanism. Supplementary coping analyses were descriptive and exploratory. These findings provide qualified empirical support for a three-factor framework of students’ responses to AI-related employment uncertainty, and highlight differences in threat-anxiety coupling across student populations. The results carry implications for targeted student support services addressing AI-related career concerns.

items.title: Generative AI‑Empowered Optimization Strategies for High School English Teaching: A Case Study of Poetry Appreciation of The Road Not Taken in Selective Compulsory Course 3
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into education and teaching, the question of how to leverage teachers' professional judgment and achieve effective human-machine collaboration has become a significant issue. Based on the theories of AI-TPACK and SAMR, this study focuses on the human-machine co-creation mechanism in the design of high school English teaching activities supported by generative AI. The research employs semi-structured interviews and design-based research methods. By interviewing three high school English teachers, their AI-TPACK performance and practical dilemmas are analyzed. Subsequently, a human-machine co-creation teaching operation model is constructed, and two rounds of practice are carried out in a high school English poetry appreciation course. The research findings indicate that teachers have developed a certain awareness of AI integration, yet they still encounter problems such as poor adaptation to students' learning situations, insufficient output evaluation, and inadequate collaboration mechanisms. The practice shows that continuous negotiation, evaluation, and reconstruction under teachers' guidance are the keys to achieving effective human-machine co-creation.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence and foreign language learning
items.abstract: Abstract Prior studies exploring teachers’ perceptions of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot, and Gemini have signaled tensions between instructors’ perceptions of GenAI’s usefulness and their beliefs regarding its ethicality. The current study furthers this line of inquiry, examining issues of ethics and utility by focusing specifically on teachers of languages other than English. Using a sequential mixed-methods design, this study employed a survey to understand language instructors’ ( N = 101) perceptions of the ethicality of GenAI tool use in higher education, along with their perceptions of the usefulness of GenAI for supporting second language (L2) learning. Semi-structured interviews were then conducted with six teachers to further understand participants’ survey responses, with some teachers sharing additional artifacts (e.g., course policies regarding GenAI). The findings suggest that most teachers (92.1%) believe GenAI tools are ethical if used for specific purposes. There also appears to be a connection between teachers’ ethical beliefs and their perceptions of GenAI’s utility, in terms of whether GenAI is used by students as a scaffold/support mechanism versus being used to produce content. The implications of this study provide a roadmap for developing discipline-specific guidelines that preserve L2 learning integrity while leveraging GenAI’s utility.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Midwifery Workforce Development
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly explored across health care for clinical decision-making and education. Within digital health, workforce readiness and digital capability are recognized as critical to successful technology implementation. Midwifery faces persistent workforce challenges including limited protected learning time, restricted leadership development opportunities, and unclear career pathways, yet it is unclear whether generative AI has been examined as a tool to support midwifery workforce development. A scoping review was conducted following the framework of Arksey and O’Malley with PRISMA-ScR reporting. EBSCOhost (CINAHL, MEDLINE, ERIC), Google Scholar, and Elicit were searched for English-language studies published between 2015 and 2026 examining AI in midwifery in relation to at least one of the following: post-registration education, workforce, professional development, leadership, and career progression. Findings were synthesized using framework analysis. Eight studies met the inclusion criteria. Research focused predominantly on clinical decision-making, predictive models, and undergraduate education. No studies examined generative AI tools to support practicing midwives’ professional development, leadership, or career progression. Attitudes towards AI varied with digital literacy, generational cohort, and ethical concerns. Generative AI in midwifery workforce development is unexamined in the empirical literature. Further research is required to understand acceptability, risks, and value within an ethically governed implementation framework.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence use and interpersonal educational interaction among nursing students: self-regulated learning as a statistical mediator
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is reshaping health sciences education. For nursing students, educational interaction (EI), self-regulated learning (SRL), and GAI interaction are all particularly important. However, these relationships and their processes remain underexplored. Methods A total of 1020 nursing students were recruited from one medical university in Hunan Province in China. The Demographics Questionnaire, the Chinese version of Student-GAI interaction scale, the Educational Interaction Scale, and the Self-regulated Learning Questionnaire were administered. SPSS 22.0 and AMOS 24.0 software were used to analyze the data. Results The mean scores of student-GAI interaction (SGI) and EI were 14.80 ± 2.27 and 70.90 ± 8.15, respectively. Significant positive relationships were found among all three variables (all P < 0.01). Both SGI (β = 0.256) and SRL (β = 0.520) positively were associated with EI (both P < 0.001). Furthermore, SGI showed a significant direct association with EI, with a direct effect value of 0.92 ( P < 0.001). SRL statistically mediated the association between SGI and EI, with a significant indirect effect value of 0.44. The mediating effect represented 32.35% of the total effect ( P < 0.001). Dimension-specific analyses revealed that the mediating effect was strongest for student-teacher interaction (45.41%) and student-content interaction (41.54%). Conclusions SGI is positively associated with EI among nursing students, both directly and indirectly through SRL. Educational strategies that encourage effective GAI use and strengthen SRL may be associated with enhanced EI in nursing education.

items.title: Governing Artificial Intelligence in Sports Science Academia
items.abstract: This chapter examines the governance of Artificial Intelligence in Sports Science academia, emphasizing the intersection of regulatory frameworks, educational practice, and academic integrity. It argues that AI governance in sport must extend beyond general data protection and transparency concerns to address domain-specific risks related to athlete welfare, informed consent, and high-stakes decision-making. The chapter presents a comparative analysis of global regulatory models, including the European Union’s risk-based approach, the United States’ soft-law framework, and diverse Asian and South American strategies, highlighting their implications for academic research and data governance in sport contexts. Further, the chapter explores the integration of AI governance into academic publishing and higher education, outlining converging principles such as human accountability, mandatory disclosure of AI use, and the prohibition of AI authorship. It introduces a harmonic model of AI integration based on active use, critical supervision, and epistemic accountability, positioning AI as a supportive but inherently fallible tool. The chapter also conceptualizes AI literacy as a core competence in sports science education and proposes a structured curriculum governance framework that integrates ethical reasoning, uncertainty interpretation, and responsible AI use. Collectively, the chapter provides a comprehensive foundation for aligning technological innovation with regulatory compliance, educational transformation, and the preservation of scientific integrity in Sports Science.

items.title: GRADUS: Discovering and Recovering Agent Lessons from the Environment's Latent Syllabus
items.abstract: Training LLM agents for policy-constrained tool environments, such as an airline backend with booking, refund, and cancellation policies, requires tasks that exercise the environment's rules individually and in combination. Existing synthesis pipelines let a model propose tasks and retain only those it immediately solves, biasing training data toward easier behaviors. We introduce Gradus (Graded Rungs of Ascending Difficulty from an Underlying System), which decouples what a task should teach from the concrete task and solution used to teach it. Without seed tasks, Gradus treats a fixed environment as a latent syllabus, extracting guarded behavioral operators that capture how actions depend on current conditions and how their effects reshape subsequent decisions. It composes these operators into increasingly demanding tasks while using corpus-level feedback to target missing outcome combinations. Crucially, Gradus jointly calibrates tasks and solutions against the environment: execution feedback identifies which side to refine while preserving the intended behavioral requirements. Verification thus becomes a recovery signal rather than a terminal filter, coupling coverage-guided exploration with the preservation of difficult examples. From off-the-shelf backbones, the resulting curriculum lifts a 30B model from 59% to 89% on $τ^2$-Bench and from 47% to 83% on CAR-Bench with an Opus 4.5 proposer, and to 76% and 62%, respectively, with an open-weight Qwen3-235B proposer. These results show the value of jointly controlling which behaviors are explored and which survive into verified training data.

items.title: Groundhog Loops: A Time-Loop Testbed for Measuring Learning Speed and Tactic Formation in AI Agents
items.abstract: The project defines a test environment inspired by the time-loop mechanism featured in the film Groundhog Day. An agent attempts to complete a task; if it makes an error classified as fatal (or exhausts its step budget), the environment is restored to a previously saved checkpoint, while the agent retains a complete, structured memory of all previous loops: the loop counter, cumulative time, summaries of failed attempts, and its own hypotheses. Unlike a conventional episode reset in reinforcement learning (RL), failure information is not lost—it becomes a persistent part of the agent's observations. Additionally, after a reset, the environment may slightly mutate the task conditions, but only when necessary to force the agent to change its strategy (the minimal-intervention principle). These mutations are observable to the agent but are never explicitly signaled. Project objectives: - C1. Build a measurable benchmark for agents' ability to perform within-episode meta-learning (in-context adaptation across resets): the agent should learn from failures without updating its weights. - C2. Investigate whether explicit loop memory reduces time to success compared with an agent without memory (control-group experiments). - C3. Investigate whether minimal changes to task conditions disrupt strategy lock-in, i.e., a situation in which an agent repeatedly attempts variations of the same flawed strategy despite having complete memory of its failures. - C4. Provide a reproducible, deterministic (seeded) harness for experiments with RL agents and LLM-based agents, using a single, unified evaluation protocol. - C5. Identify and measure undesirable emergent behaviors: reward hacking through deliberately triggering resets, learned helplessness, and overfitting to the mutation pattern. Out of scope: gradient-based weight training across loops (the project evaluates in-context adaptation through memory, not through-gradient meta-learning); physical real-time simulation. Artifacts: github.com/casual-art/Groudhog-Day (harness, docs); archive DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23483377.

items.title: Hacia una ética proléptica: experiencia, anticipación e inteligencia artificial
items.abstract: This article presents the results of a theoretical-conceptual study based on a critical analysis of the relevant philosophical literature. The central concepts were traced across the philosophical literature and, on the basis of that analysis, ethical prolepsis is proposed as an attitude of the operative subject toward the foreseeable consequences of their actions, an attitude grounded in accumulated experience and constitutively practical in its orientation, that is, always referred to effective courses of action rather than to formal principles detached from praxis. It is found that, although the anticipatory disposition can be identified at various points in the Western philosophical tradition, it has in no case received a formulation that situates it as an ethical attitude of primary standing, and it is precisely that omission which this work aims to help redress. As part of the proposal, the manifestations of the proleptic attitude are established at the individual and social levels, and its specific relevance to the phenomenon of artificial intelligence (AI) is argued, with attention to the problem of anthropomorphization, whose epistemic and moral consequences are briefly examined in relation to epistemic agency, moral agency, responsibility gaps, and biocomputation.

items.title: Hearsay or Fact? How Framing and Elicitation Shape LLM Probability Updates
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judgment assistants and as stand-in participants in psychology experiments, yet little is known about how much their probability estimates move in response to a single new piece of information. We pair premise-hypothesis items from $δ$-SNLI with one strengthener and one weakener each, elicit the prior and the posteriors in separate calls, and measure the directional movement s: the mean posterior change signed by the annotated direction, so that the prior cancels out. We vary whether the update is stated ("Here is something else you learned") or reported ("Someone said that"), and whether the model gives one probability or five weighted estimates. We test seven configurations: two local models (Qwen3-8B, OLMo-2-7B; 240 pairs) and five configurations run through agent command-line harnesses (120 pairs), with hypotheses and analysis rules fixed before the formal runs (not publicly registered). Under stated, direct elicitation all seven move in the annotated direction (s = 18-28 percentage points). Reporting lowers s in all seven point estimates (significantly in six, by 2-5 points) and raises the share of reverse movements in all seven: the effect is consistent but small. Five weighted estimates lower the share of responses at $\leq$5% or $\geq$95% in all seven, but in the two local models they also reduce s by 43% and 68%, whereas in the harnessed configurations the point estimates of the change lie between -3.7 and +0.5 points. An elicitation format that reduces extreme values thus need not preserve sensitivity to evidence; the two should be tested separately. Because $δ$-NLI annotates only direction, we make no claim about how large an update should be. Code, data and the frozen plan: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies

items.title: Heaviness–Location Congruency Improves Search Efficiency in Digital Menu Interfaces
items.abstract: This research examines whether heaviness-location congruency, a sensory correspondence between heaviness and spatial position, improves search performance and usability in digital café menus. Two experiments tested this principle using a simplified two-item selection task and a grid-based menu interface. Experiment 2 assessed effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction and included exploratory eye-tracking analyses. The clearest effect emerged in Experiment 2: congruent layouts enabled faster known-target searches than incongruent and realistic control layouts. Accuracy, subjective time, and satisfaction did not differ significantly between the three interface groups. Composite usability scores (SUM) also showed a significant overall group effect, primarily reflecting the efficiency-related measures of reaction time and subjective time. Exploratory eye-tracking results were broadly consistent with the behavioral findings, with the clearest group difference in the on-target fixation ratio. These findings suggest that heaviness-location congruency may facilitate known-target search efficiency in digital menu interfaces, although benefits for other usability dimensions were not established.

items.title: How Can AI Enhance the Sourcing Capabilities of Small and Medium Sized Art Auction Houses
items.abstract: Against the backdrop of profound structural shifts within the global art-auction ecosystem, small- and medium-sized auction houses (SMEs) are confronted with multi-faceted sourcing dilemmas. These include the growing scarcity of high-quality uncirculated artworks ("fresh lots"), diminishing returns from traditional sourcing channels, mounting compliance burdens brought by updated cultural relic regulations, and persistent competitive disadvantages against internationally leading auction institutions. Conventional sourcing workflows rely heavily on personal social networks and individual expert experience, leading to fragmented information storage and limited capacity to expand beyond existing client circles. Although existing academic papers have explored AI-driven artwork valuation, research focusing on AI-assisted upstream sourcing procedures for resource-constrained SME auction houses remains underdeveloped. This paper adopts the Gioia-style grounded-theory inductive qualitative methodology, drawing on five semi-structured in-depth interviews with core practitioners from auction institutions located in the Yangtze River Delta region of China. Through three-phase coding procedures, four aggregate theoretical dimensions are extracted: systemic root causes of sourcing difficulties, fundamental transformation of channel operation logic, structural differentiation of collector behaviours and mindsets, as well as the value boundaries and practical obstacles for AI implementation. Based on these empirical findings, this study constructs an embedded five-stage closed-loop human-AI collaborative sourcing scheme. Different from high-cost custom-built technical systems, the proposed solution adopts zero-code off-the-shelf tooling, explicitly positioning artificial intelligence as an information-augmentation instrument rather than a complete substitute for human professional judgment and trust-based interpersonal negotiation. This research enriches existing literature concerning digital transformation within the art market and delivers context-aware, actionable operational suggestions for SME auction practitioners with limited technical and financial budgets.

items.title: How L2 selves shape attitudes toward AI-assisted language learning: the mediating roles of intrinsic and extrinsic motivation in cross-cultural Asian contexts
items.abstract: Introduction This study investigates the relationship between the L2 motivational self-system and attitudes toward AI-enhanced second language (L2) learning, and tests whether intrinsic and extrinsic motivation mediate these relationships among students learning Chinese or English as a foreign language in Thailand, Macau, and Mainland China. Methods Questionnaire data were collected from 361 participants. Correlational analysis, hierarchical regression, and a bootstrapping approach were used to test mediational relations. Results Both the ought-to L2 self and the ideal L2 self were significantly associated with attitudes toward AI-enhanced L2 learning, with the ideal L2 self showing the stronger association. In the overall sample, and in the Thai and Mainland Chinese samples analyzed separately, intrinsic and extrinsic motivation statistically fully mediated the association between the ought-to L2 self and attitudes toward AI-enhanced L2 learning. In the Macau sample, extrinsic motivation was more involved than intrinsic motivation in transmitting this effect. For the ideal L2 self, intrinsic and extrinsic motivation only partially mediated the relationship with attitudes toward AI-enhanced L2 learning. Discussion Positive attitudes toward AI-enhanced L2 learning are not formed merely through future self-representations; they are also linked to learners’ intrinsic and extrinsic motivation. By examining the interaction between the L2 motivational self-system and intrinsic and extrinsic motivation across different regions, this study extends L2 motivation research to the area of AI-enhanced language learning.

items.title: How visual and auditory task loads differently impair the advantage of multimodal warnings
items.abstract: Multimodal warnings elicit faster response times than unisensory warnings in cockpits. However, how visual and auditory task demands affect the detection of multimodal warnings remains unclear. This study recruited 30 pilots and 30 control participants to complete a warning response task and an aviation visual or auditory task. The race model inequality analysis indicated that the multisensory enhancement effect decreased as the load increased. The analysis of variance indicated an interaction effect among modality, load level, and task type on response times. Results suggested that demanding tasks may affect the detection of multimodal warnings more substantially than that of unisensory warnings within the same modality. The slowing of response times to multimodal warnings may be driven by the more load-sensitive sensory component. The findings were consistent across groups. This study provides practical implications for multimodal warning design and theoretical insights into multimodal processing.
